title: Tools for Following Cells and Genes

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Codex accuracy gate and fixes

cards.front: In the developmental toolkit of this lesson, what decides the strongest claim a method can support?
cards.back: The event the tool records or changes. A method's claim reaches no further than that event: detection, transport, DNA synthesis, inherited DNA change, deletion or imposed activity.
cards.why: "Strongest claim" means the direct claim under the tested conditions, not a full account of the biology.
cards.quote: the event a tool records or changes sets the strongest claim it can support

cards.front: An antibody binds its target in a tissue section. What is the strongest direct claim?
cards.back: That the target was detected there. Protein binding reports detection, not function and not the cell's identity.
cards.quote: protein binding reports detection of a molecular target

cards.front: A {{c1::Nissl}} stain binds the RNA-rich cytoplasm around a nucleus, so it shows cell bodies across a section.
cards.back: Good for counting cells and finding the boundaries of layers. It also shows glial nuclei and some proximal dendrite.
cards.quote: A Nissl stain binds the RNA-rich cytoplasm around a nucleus, so it shows cell bodies across a section
cards.section: What is this cell, and where does it connect?

cards.front: A {{c1::Golgi}} stain fills a small, unpredictable fraction of cells completely, including their dendrites.
cards.back: So you see the whole shape of a few neurons against a clear background.
cards.quote: A Golgi stain fills a small, unpredictable fraction of cells completely, including their dendrites
cards.section: What is this cell, and where does it connect?

cards.front: In one brain section you must count cells and find the boundaries of cortical layers; in another you must draw the full dendritic tree of a few neurons. Which classical stain for each, and why?
cards.back: Nissl for the counting and the layer boundaries, because it marks cell bodies across the whole section. Golgi for the dendritic trees, because it fills a few cells completely against a clear background.
cards.why: Golgi fills an unpredictable fraction, so it cannot be used to count; Nissl shows little of the dendrites.
cards.quote: so you see the whole shape of a few neurons against a clear background
cards.section: What is this cell, and where does it connect?

cards.front: What does immunostaining report about a cell?
cards.back: Whether one chosen protein, the antibody's target, was detected there. Nothing more.
cards.quote: Immunostaining uses an antibody against one chosen protein, so it reports whether that molecular target was detected
cards.section: What is this cell, and where does it connect?

cards.front: An antibody that detects the mouse version of a protein gives no signal in a chick section. Does that prove chick cells lack the protein?
cards.back: No. The antibody may not recognize the chick version, or the single site it recognizes may be masked. A negative detection result is not by itself evidence that the target is absent.
cards.quote: an antibody raised against a mouse protein may not recognize the chick version
cards.section: What is this cell, and where does it connect?

cards.front: Injected into a region, an {{c1::anterograde}} tracer such as biotinylated dextran amine is carried toward the terminals of neurons there.
cards.back: It reports where those cells project.
cards.quote: Inject an anterograde tracer such as biotinylated dextran amine into a region
cards.section: What is this cell, and where does it connect?

cards.front: Fluorogold is injected into a target region of a brain. Which cells end up labelled, and what does that show?
cards.back: Cell bodies whose terminals took up enough tracer in that region. Terminals carry it back, so the label marks neurons that project to the injected target.
cards.quote: Inject Fluorogold into a target instead, and terminals carry it back to cell bodies
cards.section: What is this cell, and where does it connect?

cards.front: A tracer is injected into region A and labelled cell bodies appear in region B. What must be established before concluding that B projects to A?
cards.back: The direction that tracer travels. Cholera toxin B subunit, for example, moves both ways, so direction has to be established for each tracer before cell-body label is read as a projection to the injection site.
cards.quote: Cholera toxin B subunit travels both ways and is used mainly retrogradely, so direction must be established for each tracer
cards.section: What is this cell, and where does it connect?

cards.front: Why does a dye injection not reveal one neuron's synaptic partners, and which tool in this lesson goes a defined step further?
cards.back: A dye injection labels a population, so it gives population wiring rather than one cell's synapses. A rabies virus restricted to one synaptic step labels cells directly presynaptic to a defined starter population, or even to one starter cell.
cards.quote: Either dye injection gives population wiring, not one cell's synapses
cards.section: What is this cell, and where does it connect?

cards.front: Tritiated thymidine, and later the thymidine analog {{c1::BrdU}}, use DNA replication as a clock.
cards.back: Both are incorporated wherever DNA is being synthesized, which in a dividing cell means S phase.
cards.quote: Tritiated thymidine, and later the thymidine analog BrdU, use DNA replication as a clock

cards.front: After a thymidine-analog pulse in proliferating tissue, why does heavy residual label approximately date a cell's last S phase?
cards.back: Each further division usually dilutes the label among descendants, so a cell that still holds a lot of label has divided few times since the pulse.
cards.quote: each further division usually dilutes label among descendants

cards.front: A BrdU-positive nucleus turns up in injured tissue whose cells are thought not to divide. Must that cell have passed through S phase?
cards.back: No. Thymidine analogues can also enter DNA during repair. In a dividing cell S phase is the main interpretation, but BrdU alone does not separate repair from replication here; cell-cycle evidence and the context are needed.
cards.quote: Thymidine analogues can also enter DNA during repair

cards.front: In the same labelled cortex, one nucleus is heavily labelled and another weakly labelled. What does each support, and what caveat applies?
cards.back: Heavy label supports few additional divisions after the pulse; weak label is consistent with continued cycling. The caveat is that uptake and detection also vary between cells.
cards.quote: Heavy residual label supports few additional divisions; weak label is consistent with continued cycling

cards.front: What does a thymidine-analog "birthday" not tell you about a neuron?
cards.back: It is not an exact timestamp and it is no readout of cell identity. It is an approximate last S phase.
cards.quote: an approximate last S phase, not an exact timestamp or a readout of cell identity

cards.front: A progenitor is fully labelled by a BrdU pulse and then divides three more times, with the label split evenly at each division. What fraction of the original label does one great-grandchild carry?
cards.back: One eighth, about 12.5 percent. Setup: each division halves the label, so after three divisions the share is (1/2)^3 = 1/8 = 0.125. This is why a weakly labelled nucleus is consistent with continued cycling.
cards.why: Rests on the lesson's rule that each further division dilutes label among descendants; even splitting is the simplest case.
cards.quote: After a pulse in proliferating tissue, each further division usually dilutes label among descendants

cards.front: A pregnant mouse gets tritiated thymidine on embryonic day 11. One animal is fixed an hour later and the label sits in the proliferative zone beside the ventricle; littermates fixed ten days after birth show heavily labelled nuclei in the deepest cortex. Why is the one-hour animal needed?
cards.back: It shows where the label entered DNA: in dividing cells beside the ventricle.
cards.quote: They are incorporated wherever DNA is being synthesized, which in a dividing cell means S phase

cards.front: In quail-chick grafting, what makes a quail cell recognizable in a chick host long after it has migrated?
cards.back: Its nucleus. Quail nuclei carry a distinctive condensed-chromatin pattern that survives migration and differentiation.
cards.quote: Quail nuclei carry a distinctive condensed-chromatin pattern, so quail cells grafted into a chick embryo stay recognizable in sections

cards.front: A quail neural tube is grafted into a chick embryo, and quail-marked cells later appear in a peripheral ganglion. What does that establish?
cards.back: Ancestry: those ganglion cells descend from the graft rather than the host. A durable mark passed to daughter cells reports whose descendant a cell is.
cards.quote: The marker shows that the marked cells descend from the graft

cards.front: Quail-derived cells are found in a chick peripheral ganglion. Does the marker show that the host contributed no ganglion cells, or which signals the cells needed?
cards.back: Neither. Unmarked host cells may also contribute, and no signal was manipulated, so the graft reveals no requirement. It also cannot report the potential of any single founder.
cards.quote: Unmarked host cells may also contribute, and the graft does not by itself reveal which signals were required

cards.front: Why does every descendant of a retrovirally labelled progenitor stay marked?
cards.back: The retrovirus integrates its genome into the DNA of the dividing cell, so the insert and its marker gene are copied with the genome and inherited by all daughters.
cards.quote: A retrovirus integrates its genome into the DNA of a dividing cell, so every descendant of that cell inherits the insert

cards.front: A retroviral labelling experiment uses a high viral dose, and clusters of marked cells are counted as clones. What goes wrong?
cards.back: Labelled clones can overlap, so one cluster may hold the descendants of several founders. The one-cluster-one-progenitor reading is a sampling argument that depends on a dose low enough to keep clones apart.
cards.quote: That assumption is a sampling argument, not an observation, and it is where this method can fail

cards.front: A Cre-dependent reporter commonly places a {{c1::loxP-flanked transcriptional stop}} before a fluorescent protein gene.
cards.back: Other designs leave the gene inverted until Cre flips it.
cards.quote: A Cre-dependent reporter commonly places a loxP-flanked transcriptional stop before a fluorescent protein gene

cards.front: Once Cre has deleted the stop in a reporter allele, why is the label inherited, and what can still switch it off?
cards.back: The recombined allele is a change in DNA, so it passes to descendants. The cells stay labelled only as long as the reporter's promoter is active.
cards.quote: When Cre recombinase deletes the stop, the recombined allele passes to descendants

cards.front: A cell-type Cre crossed to one single-colour reporter marks thousands of cells. Why can that not resolve single families, and what three changes would let you follow one?
cards.back: One colour over many founders gives a population fate map, not separate clones, because neighbouring families look identical. Following one family needs sparse or low-dose induction, multicolour reporters, or founder-specific barcodes.
cards.quote: Following one family requires sparse or low-dose induction, multicolour reporters, or founder-specific barcodes

cards.front: In an invented clonal culture, single migratory cells are plated one per well. Of 1,743 cells seeded, 190 colonies appear; 17 are excluded for lacking the marker panel. Of the 173 analyzed clones, 76 hold a neuronal marker, and each of those 76 also holds non-neuronal cells. What fraction of analyzed clones is mixed, and what does it support?
cards.back: About 44 percent. Setup: 190 − 17 = 173 analyzed clones; 76/173 = 0.439, so about 44 percent are mixed neuronal plus non-neuronal. That supports some single founders making several cell types. Dividing by the 1,743 seeded instead gives about 4 percent and mixes denominators.
cards.why: Rests on the lesson's rule that a durable mark, here one founder per well, reports descent from that founder.
cards.quote: A durable mark passes to daughter cells

cards.front: In classical gene targeting, how does an engineered sequence end up in the target gene's own place?
cards.back: DNA matching the gene on both sides of the intended change is supplied to mouse embryonic stem cells. In rare cells, homologous recombination swaps the new version into the locus itself.
cards.quote: In rare cells, homologous recombination swaps the new version into the gene's own place

cards.front: Classical targeting selects twice: a marker inside the construct and a thymidine kinase gene outside the matching arms. What does each selection do, and what is still required?
cards.back: The positive marker inside keeps cells that took up DNA. The thymidine kinase outside the arms makes ganciclovir lethal, killing most cells that inserted the whole construct at random and kept it. Survivors still require genotyping.
cards.why: Correct homologous recombination does not incorporate the outside marker; random insertion keeps it.
cards.quote: A positive marker inside the construct retains cells that took up DNA

cards.front: Destroying a gene is a knockout; writing in a sequence such as a fluorescent reporter is a {{c1::knock-in}}.
cards.quote: Destroying a gene is a knockout; writing in a sequence such as a fluorescent reporter is a knock-in

cards.front: Targeted embryonic stem cells are put into an early embryo. What is the resulting pup called, and when is the new allele heritable?
cards.back: The pup is a chimera. The allele is heritable if the targeted cells made its gametes.
cards.quote: The pup is a chimera, and the allele is heritable if those cells made its gametes

cards.front: Give two limits of a straight whole-body knockout as a way to ask what a gene does.
cards.back: It can kill the embryo before the question matters, and whole-body deletion cannot identify which tissue mattered.
cards.quote: A straight knockout can kill an embryo before the question matters, and whole-body deletion cannot identify the tissue that mattered

cards.front: In mouse genotype notation, what do a superscript and a slash each mean? Read p75NTR-/- and DR6+/-.
cards.back: A superscript names what is written at a locus; a slash separates its alleles. So p75NTR-/- is a homozygous knockout and DR6+/- a heterozygote.
cards.quote: A superscript names what is written at a locus; a slash separates its alleles

cards.front: Read the genotype AvilCre/+;TrkAfl/-. Which gene is lost, and in which cells?
cards.back: Advillin drives Cre on one allele; the floxed TrkA copy is the only potentially functional copy, so cutting it leaves none. TrkA is therefore deleted wherever this Avil-Cre is active: sensory neurons and also some sympathetic, parasympathetic and enteric neurons.
cards.quote: The floxed TrkA copy is the only potentially functional copy available to lose

cards.front: A full CreER, floxed-gene and reporter mouse is given vehicle instead of tamoxifen. Which failure does that test?
cards.back: Ligand-independent CreER activity: recombination happening although the inducing drug was withheld. If the reporter lights up on vehicle, the timing of deletion cannot be trusted.
cards.quote: It tests ligand-independent CreER activity: recombination when the inducing drug was withheld

cards.front: A schematic of a conditional cross looks clean. Which two driver failures can it not show, and what must be measured in the real animals?
cards.back: Leakiness, recombining where or when it should not, and mosaicism, recombining in only some target cells. Measure the driver's range and how much target protein is actually lost, in the tissue, ages and animals used; reporter light cannot quantify residual protein.
cards.quote: Measure the driver's range and the target's loss in the tissue, ages and animals used

cards.front: A single Cre driver recombines in your target cells but also in two neighbouring classes. How does intersectional targeting narrow this, and why does it work?
cards.back: Add a second recombinase, Flp, with its own sites, and run two independent switches. Requiring both in the same cell increases specificity, because only cells in the overlap of the two expression patterns are recombined.
cards.quote: Intersectional targeting adds a second recombinase, Flp, with its own sites and runs two independent switches

cards.front: Gene X is needed for embryonic survival, so a straight knockout dies before birth. You want what X does in sensory neurons after birth. List the alleles, the drug, the reporter and three controls.
cards.back: A sensory-neuron CreER driver, X floxed over floxed, and a Cre-dependent reporter; tamoxifen after birth so X survives embryogenesis; the reporter marks cells where Cre was active. Controls: CreER with no floxed allele plus tamoxifen; floxed over floxed with no CreER plus tamoxifen; the full genotype on vehicle.
cards.why: The three controls test Cre-plus-tamoxifen damage, a hypomorphic floxed allele, and ligand-independent recombination.
cards.quote: Give tamoxifen after birth to preserve X through embryonic development and trigger deletion later

cards.front: A conditional knockout gives a mild phenotype, but reporter-positive cells still contain much of the target protein. How does that change the interpretation?
cards.back: The mild phenotype may reflect incomplete deletion rather than a small role for the gene. Phenotype size depends on how much protein is actually gone, so residual protein must be measured in reporter-positive cells before the gene is called unimportant.
cards.quote: measure how much X protein is actually gone in reporter-positive cells, because phenotype size depends on it

cards.front: {{c1::Necessary}} means you removed it and the outcome failed.
cards.quote: Necessary means you removed it and the outcome failed

cards.front: {{c1::Sufficient}} means you added the thing and the outcome followed.
cards.back: Necessity and sufficiency can each hold without the other.
cards.quote: Sufficient means you added the thing and the outcome followed

cards.front: Overexpressing protein A makes structure B expand, but knocking out A leaves B unchanged. Is A necessary, sufficient under the tested conditions, both, or neither?
cards.back: Sufficient under those conditions, not necessary for this outcome. The gain-of-function may place A at levels or locations it never normally reaches, and a redundant relative may cover its loss.
cards.quote: The gain-of-function may place A at levels or locations it never normally reaches

cards.front: What is the difference between a reporter and an actuator, with one example of each?
cards.back: A reporter reads out a state: a calcium sensor brightens when calcium rises. An actuator imposes a state: blue light opens channelrhodopsin and drives firing.
cards.quote: A reporter reads out a state: a fluorescent protein marks where a cell is

cards.front: Which light-gated tool drives firing, and which suppresses activity, in the pair named in this lesson?
cards.back: Blue light opens channelrhodopsin, a cation channel, to drive firing. Yellow light drives halorhodopsin to move chloride and suppress activity.
cards.quote: yellow light drives halorhodopsin to move chloride and suppress activity

cards.front: You want to test whether firing one class of interneuron in a mouse is enough to stop grooming. Which genetic tool do those cells need, and why not a calcium sensor?
cards.back: An actuator: a light-gated cation channel expressed from a cell-specific Cre-dependent allele, so only those cells can be driven on command. A calcium sensor only reports activity and cannot impose it, so it cannot test sufficiency.
cards.quote: An actuator can ask whether that activity is enough

cards.front: A chemical actuator puts TRPV1, a capsaicin-gated channel, into chosen neurons. Why is the mouse's own TRPV1 knocked out first?
cards.back: So that capsaicin activates only the chosen neurons. With the native channel still present, the drug would also act on the animal's own TRPV1-expressing cells and the manipulation would not be cell-specific.
cards.quote: Put TRPV1, a capsaicin-gated channel, into chosen neurons of a mouse whose own TRPV1 is knocked out

cards.front: Calcium imaging shows a neuron class active just before a behaviour. What claim does that support, and what does it not?
cards.back: It supports that the activity goes with the outcome. It does not show that the activity caused it; an activity reporter reads out a state, so an actuator is needed to ask whether the activity is enough.
cards.quote: An activity reporter alone shows that activity goes with an outcome, not that it caused it

cards.front: An antibody detects protein P in heavily BrdU-labelled deep-layer neurons, and a cell-type Cre reporter marks the same cells. A colleague concludes P is required for those neurons to settle in the deep layer. What do the data support, and what is needed?
cards.back: Only detection of P there, an approximate last S phase, and descent from the marked founders. Necessity is untested because nothing was removed; it needs a conditional deletion of P in those cells, with the deletion and the residual protein measured.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that the event a tool records sets its strongest claim: deletion, not detection, tests necessity.
cards.quote: deletion tests necessity, and imposed activity tests sufficiency

cards.front: How can carbon-14 date when a human cell last made its DNA?
cards.back: Atmospheric nuclear weapons testing raised carbon-14 sharply before the 1963 test ban treaty, after which it fell, so the carbon-14 in a cell's genomic DNA reflects the year that DNA was last made.
cards.quote: A cell's genomic-DNA carbon-14 therefore reflects the year its DNA was last made

cards.front: How did CRISPR shorten the path to a new mouse allele, compared with classical targeting?
cards.back: A guide RNA brings Cas9 nuclease to a matching sequence in a fertilized egg, so many alleles can be built without embryonic stem cells or chimeras.
cards.quote: a guide RNA brings Cas9 nuclease to a matching sequence in a fertilized egg
cards.section: From classical targeting to newer routes
